phonemes.desc: Smooth breathing; short epsilon opens the name without aspiration.
Single rho, a liquid that rolls between the vowels.
Long omega [ɔː], the sustained note at the end — desire prolonged.

pronunciation.approximation: "EH-ross" — the accent falls on the first syllable; the o of the second is held longer than English allows, deep and sustained.

pronunciation.note: Érōs is Tier 1 because the Greek Ἔρως contains both stress (acute on the initial epsilon) and length (the long omega). The acute on the initial É preserves the stress, while the macron on the final ō preserves the long vowel. The name is the full scholarly form of the force that moves the cosmos.

domains.title: Desire
domains.subtitle: Attraction, Union, Cosmic Motion
domains.lead: Érōs is not merely romance. He is the attraction that makes things move toward each other: fire upward, water downward, god toward mortal, atom toward atom. In the earliest Greek cosmogonies, Érōs is a primordial power; only later does he become the mischievous child of Aphrodite.

cards.name: The Bow
cards.desc: His weapon makes the limbs go slack and the mind unmade; no god or mortal is immune.

cards.name: Wings
cards.desc: Desire is swift and sudden; it arrives before reason can arrange a defense.

cards.name: The Heart Aflame
cards.desc: The fire of longing — physical, spiritual, cosmic.

cards.name: The Rose
cards.desc: Flower of Aphrodite and Érōs; beauty that wounds as it invites.

mythology.lead: Érōs stands at the beginning in Hesiod and at the margins in Homer, where he serves Aphrodite as her companion but is no child of hers. He is one of the oldest gods in the Greek imagination, yet his stories are few — because his power is everywhere, and a thing that is everywhere has no need of a plot. The tradition's five great witnesses — Hesiod, Parmenides, Aristophanes, the Orphic theogonies, and Apuleius — give us not a biography but a physics of desire.

myths.title: Fourth of the Primordials
myths.text: Hesiod places Érōs fourth in the procession of being: after Cháos, Gaia, and Tartarus, but before the children of Night and the Titans — 'and Érōs, the most beautiful among the immortal gods, who loosens the limbs, and who in the breasts of all gods and of all men overcomes the intelligence and prudent counsel' (Theogony 116–122). He is generated by no one; he simply accompanies the first things into existence. The placement is the argument. Earth, pit, and desire are co-ordinate beginnings, and desire is specified with clinical precision: it does not kill, it unmakes the mind — intelligence and counsel both. Placed before gods and Titans alike, Érōs is the one force the Greeks refused to derive from anything else: union is as primitive as earth, and the catalogue of all that is cannot even begin without it.

myths.title: First of All
myths.text: In the poem of Parmenides, the goddess who teaches the young philosopher tells him that the goddess of the world 'first of all devised Érōs' among the gods (fr. B13, Diels–Kranz). The line moves Érōs from fourth to first: not one beginning among several, but the generating thought with which the cosmos was planned. Empedocles built a whole physics on the same intuition, setting Philotēs — Love, his other name for the power Aphrodite rules — against Strife as the two forces that alternately unite and scatter the four roots of things (fr. B17). In this philosophical lineage, love is not an emotion; it is a cosmological principle, the binding energy of an ordered world. The poets had always known that desire moves the stars; the philosophers' move was to make that claim without metaphor, and Érōs is the hinge on which the poem becomes the equation.

myths.title: The Cosmic Egg
myths.text: In Aristophanes' Birds (414 BCE), a comic parody of Orphic theogony, Night black-winged lays a wind-egg in the boundless folds of Erebus, and from it in the turning season hatches Érōs, 'with his back all aglitter with golden wings' — who then mates with winged Cháos in the misty clouds of Tartarus, and from the union comes the race of birds (Birds 693–702). The ornithology is a joke, but the machinery is not: egg, night, Erebus, and a self-generated desire that couples with Cháos itself — this is genuine Orphic cosmogony wearing a comic mask, older than the parody that quotes it. The image preserves the archaic idea of Érōs as an unparented power of union: he does not enter the world through a mother and a father, but hatches out of darkness carrying his own light on his back.

myths.title: The Firstborn King
myths.text: The Orphic theogonies go further than any classical source: Chronos, Time, fashions from Aither an egg, and from the egg hatches Phanēs — 'the Shining One', also called Protógonos, Firstborn, and addressed as Érōs — the primordial god who rules all and brings the hidden into light (Orphic Rhapsodies, as summarised by Damascius, De principiis). The Derveni papyrus, a fourth-century BCE commentary on an Orphic poem found in 1962, quotes the crucial episode: Zeus, intending to rule all things, 'took the god into himself' — swallowed Phanēs — 'so that the gods and all things might come to be in Zeus' (col. XII–XIII). The Orphic Hymn V invokes the god by his four names: 'O Érōs, you who rule the blessed gods and mortals.' In this theology, desire is not a member of the pantheon but its hidden engine — the first light the universe produces, and the one thing Zeus must literally contain before he can be king of anything.

myths.title: Cupid and Psyche
myths.text: In Apuleius' Latin novel The Golden Ass (books 4–6, second century CE), Érōs survives in Roman dress as Cupid, the unseen husband of Psyche — 'Soul'. An oracle dooms the mortal girl to a monster; she is carried instead to a palace in the dark where a voice she may not see loves her. Her jealous sisters persuade her to lamp-light the sleeping god; a drop of hot oil wakes him, and he flees. Psyche wanders the earth seeking him until Venus sets her impossible tasks — sorting mixed grain in a night (the ants help), gathering golden wool (a reed advises), descending to Persephone for a box of beauty (she is told not to open it, and opens it). Zeus grants the marriage; Psyche is deified, and their daughter is named Hēdonē, Pleasure. The tale belongs to Roman, not archaic Greek, tradition — it is a late antique allegory that Fulgentius already read as the soul's initiation — but it became the template for countless later stories, from 'Beauty and the Beast' to every romance of the forbidden beloved.

lore.syncretism: The Roman Cupido inherited Érōs's arrows and wings but gradually shrank from a handsome youth into a plump, blindfolded infant — the Renaissance putto. In Plato's Symposium, Érōs is redefined as the longing for beauty and the ladder from physical desire to the Form of the Good. For the Stoics, Érōs was a natural affinity (oikeiōsis) that binds the cosmos. Freud divided the psyche into Eros and Thanatos, life-drive and death-drive, making the Greek god the name of everything in us that seeks connection, pleasure, and life.
lore.culturalLegacy: Érōs is one of the most productive words in European languages: "erotic," "erogenous." He appears on Valentine's cards, in pop songs, in perfume advertisements, and in psychoanalytic theory. The image of the winged child with a bow — Cupid — is one of the most recognizable figures in Western art. Yet the archaic Érōs was more formidable: a beautiful young man who could unmake kings and gods. To restore the name Érōs with its long omega is to remember that desire is not trivial; it is one of the forces that turns the world.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Érōs is the least visible of the great powers because we experience him from inside. He is not a storm you watch from a window; he is the weather inside the room. Every longing — for a person, for a place, for a version of yourself — is a local manifestation of the same force Hesiod placed at the foundation of the cosmos.

The modern world speaks of desire mostly as consumer appetite or romantic plot. But the Greek Érōs is larger: he is the pull that holds atoms together and tears empires apart. To name him correctly is to admit that attraction is not an interruption of reason but one of its oldest engines. The heart has its own logic, and Érōs wrote it.

lore.archaeology: Numerous red-figure and black-figure vases depict Eros as a winged youth or child; the so-called Erotes appear on wedding vessels and funerary reliefs. No major sanctuary, but the Erotes were honored in gymnasia and private devotion.
